title: Gunmen, 1919 police shootings and musicians in gang-era clubs
summary: Howard tells about the shootings of two policemen in 1919, newspapers and how musicians stayed out of it.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Well he would fool us if he didn't. Did it seem like he could read music? Sure. Really? Sure.
What did Hershey Miller and Nails do? Well, they're gunmen, I guess. They were?

You know, in gang war. You know how they do. Were they pretty big time? Well they must have been, because they didn't, not one of them served a day for that. They show you what kind of town Chicago it was. The papers, it was on a Sunday morning. I'm pretty sure it was on a Sunday morning. They come out with an extra. They said they were, uh, a hundred, one thousand dollars or something like that, and wasn't booked. You know? The bonds, you know? Yeah. I go to work that afternoon at three o'clock at Dreamland and then Hershey Miller's sitting up there on the terrace reading it. No kidding.
I ain't seen that first part of Dr. J.R. leaving the police station. No kidding.
That's no kidding. Did musicians carry weapons in those days?

It didn't bother us. I forget the time Mike the Pike Hitler. What? Mike the Pike Hitler. He had a place called Wakeworm, 119th and Wood, way out south in Chicago. And they got to shooting in there one night. They asked where the band was after the shooting. Hell, I was home. I was.
I don't think anybody else did either. I'm trying to leave.
